sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Git is the tool every developer uses every day. Interviewers test whether you can collaborate on a shared codebase without creating chaos — handling branches, conflicts, and code reviews professionally. The mistakes freshers make here (pushing to main, git reset --hard, force-pushing) are visible to interviewers in take-home reviews.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
- **Working tree** → `git add` → **Staging area (index)** → `git commit` → **Local repo** → `git push` → **Remote repo**.
- A **branch** is just a pointer to a commit. Creating branches is cheap.
- **Merge** preserves history and creates a merge commit. **Rebase** rewrites commits for a linear history.
- **Merge conflict** = two people changed the same lines. Git marks it with `<<<<`, `====`, `>>>>` markers.
- **Golden rule of rebase**: never rebase branches that others are working on.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- git status / git log / git diff — know these cold, they are daily commands.
- git stash: temporary shelf for uncommitted work before switching branches.
- git reset --soft (moves HEAD, keeps index), --mixed (moves HEAD, unstages), --hard (destroys working changes — DESTRUCTIVE).
- git revert vs git reset: revert is safe (new commit), reset is destructive (rewrites history).
- PR workflow: feature branch → PR → code review → merge to main.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- "What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?" → Merge creates a merge commit and preserves history; rebase rewrites commits for a linear history.
- "How do you resolve a merge conflict?" → Find conflict markers, edit the file to keep the correct code, git add the resolved file, git commit.
- "What does git stash do?" → Saves uncommitted changes temporarily so you can switch branches and come back to them.
- "What is the difference between git pull and git fetch?" → Fetch downloads but does not integrate; pull = fetch + merge.
- "What would you do if you accidentally committed to main?" → Create a new branch from the commit, reset main to previous commit.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"In my project, I follow GitHub Flow: every feature or bug fix gets its own branch off main. When finished, I create a pull request, get a code review, and merge with a squash commit to keep the history clean. For day-to-day work I use rebase to keep my feature branch up to date with main so the final merge is a clean fast-forward. I always check git status and git log before pushing to make sure I know exactly what I'm about to send."*
